source.title: Theory of Scaling Laws for In-Context Regression: Depth, Width, Context and Time
source.authors: Blake Bordelon; Mary I. Letey; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops its own theoretical results that refine the scope of scaling laws: the exponents and compute-optimal width/depth shape depend on the ICL task statistics and model parameterization.
record.gate_note: The paper analyzes population test loss for synthetic in-context linear regression, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy. Its own asymptotic power-law results and compute-optimal width/depth relation bear on V5 and V7. Results cited from other work were not recorded. Other ICL findings, such as depth effects at finite context length and the qualitative softmax depth comparison, do not measure a power-law form or a fixed-parameter architecture comparison named by the versions.
record.test_reason: This is a solvable theory of in-context linear regression in deep linear attention, backed by simulations of trained linear transformers (Fig. 4a, 6b, 8a). It derives power-law loss in time, width, depth and context, and shows the exponents and the compute-optimal width/depth split depend on task statistics and parameterization. It is a new setting with results on V5 and V7. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss. The power laws follow from assumed power-law task spectra (source/capacity conditions).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that pretraining task statistics determine the learned solution. Under fixed covariance, the model learns a whitening preconditioner and needs no depth at infinite context, but this solution is brittle to covariance shift. Under randomly rotated covariances, the model learns general in-context gradient descent with a separable Chinchilla-like law, where width and depth can each bottleneck. The optimal shape is L ∝ N^ν, and the results are robust to reparameterizing the attention blocks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses theoretical analysis of synthetic in-context linear regression in deep linear attention, with supporting simulations; it does not reproduce the language-model pretraining experiments or held-out cross-entropy measurement of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling exponents and optimal width/depth relation depend on source/capacity exponents and task covariance structure. The time exponent also changes with the model parameterization.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss has separate additive width and depth terms (a Chinchilla-like form). Scaling only width or only depth hits a bottleneck from the other resource. At fixed compute C = tP²N²L, optimal depth scales as L ∝ N^ν.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width and depth contribute separate power-law terms, and the compute-optimal transformer shape depends on task statistics.

record.problems: Evidence is for a theoretical toy model of synthetic linear-regression ICL, not language-model pretraining or held-out language-model cross-entropy. The principal scaling results rely on stated asymptotic and source/capacity assumptions; the paper notes limitations to linear regression and linear attention in its analysis.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing directly on V5 or V7 were omitted. Other results on finite-context depth gains, fixed-covariance distribution shift, SGD batch effects, and qualitative softmax depth gains were left out because they do not report a power-law loss or the resource-allocation result named by these versions.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token counts. The paper derives only a width/depth split for a toy model.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count. Depth here is looped, with tied weights, so it does not change the parameter count.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes. Softmax experiments (Fig. 6c, 9) show only that depth helps, with no fitted power law.
Parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, training schedules, and empirical curvature away from a single power law.

missing.what: In the ISO and FS settings, depth beyond L=1 gives no benefit at infinite context, so there is no depth scaling law. All depths converge as the same power law in t.
Width-only and depth-only scaling plateau at the other resource's bottleneck, while joint scaling improves monotonically with compute.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is theoretical plus small simulations. The power laws are produced by assumed power-law spectra, so they show the form arises under those assumptions rather than empirically. The tranche was changed from T5 to T3: the paper extends scaling laws to a new setting rather than arguing against a version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss in language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token counts as functions of compute. The paper instead derives a width/depth shape relation for a toy ICL model.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
The paper tests synthetic ICL linear-regression training, not image/video modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, transfer, or language-model pretraining.
Downstream-task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The paper shows dependence on task statistics and model parameterization, but does not compare parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, or training schedules, nor test whether curves bend away from a single power law in empirical language-model runs.

rows.subject: reduced-Γ model
rows.operation_detail: Derives the pretraining-time power law for fixed structured covariances in the large-depth limit.
rows.measure: ICL population loss versus pretraining time
rows.note: The paper derives this asymptotic power law under the stated source/capacity and covariance assumptions.
rows.check: The exponent is derived in the L→∞ limit. Fig. 3b shows finite-depth models also converge as a power law in t, but with no benefit from depth. The condition should note that depth gives no scaling in the FS setting.

rows.subject: reduced-Γ model
rows.operation_detail: Derives the joint compute-optimal width/depth shape.

conditions.value: source/capacity conditions; ν controls the data spectrum

rows.measure: Compute-optimal relation between depth and width
rows.note: The authors state that the optimal relation varies with properties of the data.
rows.check: The row gives the compute-optimal depth/width relation L ∝ N^ν, not a power-law loss, so it does not bear on V5. It bears on V7 only: the optimal split depends on the data exponent ν. It is also not V3, since it allocates between width and depth, not between parameters and tokens.

rows.subject: full linear attention module
rows.operation_detail: Derives the pretraining-time loss power law for gradient flow on the attention weights separately, with read-in/readout weights fixed as specified.

conditions.value: separate attention weights; γ(t) reparameterized as w(t)^5

rows.measure: ICL population loss versus pretraining time
rows.note: The time exponent differs from the reduced-Γ model's exponent, while the loss is still expressed as a power law.

rows.subject: layer-decoupled reduced-Γ model
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes untied per-layer Γ matrices and reports their loss dynamics under gradient flow.

conditions.value: RRS, noise-free, large width and context length
all layer scale factors initialized equally

rows.measure: Loss dynamics compared with the recurrent model
rows.value: The layer scale factors remain balanced, and loss dynamics match the recurrent model when the learning rate is upscaled by L.
rows.locator: Section 5.1 and Appendix G.1, equations (117)–(118), Figure 8
rows.note: This is a stated equivalence under the specified initialization and learning-rate scaling.
rows.check: The value describes balanced layer scale factors and equivalence to the recurrent model. The power-law evidence is Fig. 8a: untied-layer loss dynamics show the same power laws. The value should cite that. The row says nothing about exponent dependence, so the V7 link is removed.

relationships.condition: Synthetic in-context linear regression (FS and RRS) with power-law task spectra; reduced-Γ, untied-layer and full linear-attention models
relationships.reason: Derived power laws in time, width, depth and context are matched by simulations of trained models (R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R7, R8).
relationships.display_finding: Trained-model simulations match derived power laws in training time, width, depth, and context length.

relationships.condition: ISO and FS settings at long context (α→∞)
relationships.reason: Text-based: Results 2–3 and Fig. 3b show depth gives no benefit at long context, so no depth power law exists there. Each resource law appears only when the other resources are unbounded (Fig. 5a–b bottlenecks). No row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Depth gave no benefit in the long-context limit, and individual resource power laws emerged only when the other resources were unbounded.

relationships.condition: Toy ICL settings with differing task statistics and parameterizations
relationships.reason: Exponents depend on source/capacity exponents β and ν, and differ between FS and RRS (R1 vs R2). Training the full attention weights changes the time exponent (R7 vs R2). The optimal width/depth split depends on ν (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Exponents depended on source and capacity exponents β and ν and differed between FS and RRS; training full attention weights changed the time exponent, and ν determined the optimal width–depth split.
